paper.title: Nicheformer: a foundation model for single-cell and spatial omics
paper.abstract: Tissue makeup depends on the local cellular microenvironment. Spatial single-cell genomics enables scalable and unbiased interrogation of these interactions. Here we introduce Nicheformer, a transformer-based foundation model trained on both human and mouse dissociated single-cell and targeted spatial transcriptomics data. Pretrained on SpatialCorpus-110M, a curated collection of over 57 million dissociated and 53 million spatially resolved cells across 73 tissues on cellular reconstruction, Nicheformer learns cell representations that capture spatial context. It excels in linear-probing and fine-tuning scenarios for a newly designed set of downstream tasks, in particular spatial composition prediction and spatial label prediction. Critically, we show that models trained only on dissociated data fail to recover the complexity of spatial microenvironments, underscoring the need for multiscale integration. Nicheformer enables the prediction of the spatial context of dissociated cells, allowing the transfer of rich spatial information to scRNA-seq datasets. Overall, Nicheformer sets the stage for the next generation of machine-learning models in spatial single-cell analysis.
paper.tldr: The authors built Nicheformer, a transformer pretrained on 57M dissociated and 53M spatial single-cell profiles, and found that it predicts spatial composition and labels, transfers spatial context to scRNA-seq, and outperforms models trained only on dissociated data.
paper.why: Nicheformer is a foundation model for single-cell and spatial transcriptomics that learns local tissue context from more than 110M dissociated and spatially resolved cells across 73 tissues. It shows why spatial context is essential for modeling microenvironments and can transfer spatial information to ordinary scRNA-seq data, making it broadly reusable for cell-atlas mining.

summary.tldr: Nicheformer is a 49.3M-parameter transformer pretrained on 110M cells (57.1M dissociated + 53.8M image-based spatial, human and mouse, 73 tissues) whose embeddings enable spatially aware tasks — niche/region label prediction, neighborhood composition and density prediction — and transfer of spatial context onto dissociated scRNA-seq.
summary.background: scRNA-seq requires cell dissociation, losing the local microenvironment, while existing single-cell foundation models (Geneformer, scGPT, UCE) are trained only on dissociated data and ignore spatial relationships. Joint modeling is hard because image-based spatial assays measure only hundreds to a few thousand genes and show strong technology-specific batch effects versus dissociated data.
summary.approach: The authors compiled SpatialCorpus-110M: 57.1M dissociated cells (built on CellXGene Census, 33.5M cells, plus 180 curated datasets from GEO/sfaira/HCA) and 53.8M spatial cells (MERFISH, Xenium, CosMx, ISS; 15 tissues, >10,600 sections, ~60% brain). Cells are tokenized by gene-expression rank over a shared human-mouse vocabulary of 20,310 genes (16,981 orthologous, 3,178 human-specific, 151 mouse-specific), with added context tokens for species, modality and assay, and technology-specific nonzero mean vectors for rank normalization. The model uses 12 encoder layers, 16 heads, 1,024-dim FFN, 512-dim embeddings and 1,500-token context, trained with masked-token prediction. Evaluation used linear probing and fine-tuning on new tasks: niche/region/cell-type label prediction, neighborhood composition regression (radii averaging 10/20/50/100 neighbors) and neighborhood density prediction on MERFISH mouse brain, CosMx human liver and lung, and Xenium lung and colon data.
findings: Fine-tuned and linear-probed Nicheformer beat Geneformer, scGPT, UCE, CellPLM, scVI and PCA (statistically significant, t-tests/FDR) on niche and region classification and composition regression; e.g., it correctly assigned the 9 motor-cortex-relevant cell types of 33 when transferring MERFISH brain labels to dissociated scRNA-seq.

Spatial data is essential: a model trained on only 1% spatial data outperformed models trained on three times as much dissociated data on spatial tasks, showing dissociated-only pretraining cannot recover spatial variation.

Attention analysis showed middle layers focus on gene tokens and late layers on context tokens; male-female attention differences in the mouse brain AVPV highlighted sexually dimorphic genes, 6 of the top 10 (e.g., Adgrf5, Nfib, Rgs4) not previously reported as dimorphic.
Predicted neighborhood density from expression alone reproduced known tumor effects: cancer sections had higher densities than healthy (colon 12.3 vs 10.7; lung 12.1 vs 10.7 cells per neighborhood).

Performance tracks cell-type abundance and regional specificity: the best-predicted brain cell types were abundant and spatially homogeneous, while rare midbrain/hypothalamus types had the largest errors.
summary.why: The paper demonstrates that spatial transcriptomics data is now sufficient to train spatially aware foundation models, and that dissociated-only pretraining is fundamentally insufficient for spatial tasks. For researchers in AI for multiomics it offers a concrete recipe — joint modality/species pretraining with context tokens, ortholog-gene vocabularies, rank-based tokenization — plus a reusable 110M-cell corpus and new spatial benchmark tasks.
summary.limitations: Pretraining is restricted to targeted spatial panels (hundreds to a few thousand genes), and on the underrepresented liver, linear probing fell below scVI/PCA baselines (recoverable with tissue-focused fine-tuning); PCA with many components is nearly on par for some probing tasks, and performance degrades for rare or regionally heterogeneous cell types.

also.title: A cell atlas foundation model for scalable search of similar human cells
also.abstract: Single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) has profiled hundreds of millions of human cells across organs, diseases, development, and perturbations to date. Mining these growing atlases could reveal cell-disease associations, discover cell states in unexpected tissue contexts, and relate in vivo biology to in vitro models. These require a common measure of cell similarity across the body and an efficient way to search. Here, we develop SCimilarity, a metric learning framework to learn a unified and interpretable representation that enables rapid queries of tens of millions of cell profiles from diverse studies for cells that are transcriptionally similar to an input cell profile or state. We use SCimilarity to query a 23.4 million cell atlas of 412 scRNA-seq studies for macrophage and fibroblast profiles from interstitial lung disease 1 and reveal similar cell profiles across other fibrotic diseases and tissues. The top scoring in vitro hit for the macrophage query was a 3D hydrogel system 2 , which we experimentally demonstrated reproduces this cell state. SCimilarity serves as a foundation model for single-cell profiles that enables researchers to query for similar cellular states across the human body, providing a powerful tool for generating biological insights from the Human Cell Atlas.

also.title: Decoding the sequence determinants of locus-specific DNA methylation across human tissues.
also.abstract: DNA methylation is a fundamental epigenetic modification that plays crucial roles in transcriptional regulation, cellular differentiation, and genome stability. However, how locus-specific DNA methylation is determined by intrinsic DNA sequence remains poorly understood. Here, we introduce Melody, a deep learning framework that predicts DNA methylation from 10-kb genomic sequences, enabling the integration of both local and long-range sequence signals. Across 39 human tissues, Melody accurately predicts methylation profiles and consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in whole-chromosome, hypomethylated-region, and cell-type-specific benchmarks. Melody also generalizes to methylation quantitative trait locus (meQTL) effect prediction and identifies regulatory sequence motifs associated with methylation variability. To extend prediction beyond profiled tissues, we further develop Melody-G, which incorporates single-cell RNA-seq foundation model embeddings to infer methylation states in previously unseen cell types from transcriptomic data. Together, Melody provides a unified framework for linking genomic sequence and cellular state to DNA methylation and offers new insights into the regulatory logic governing the human methylome.

also.title: GeneCompass: deciphering universal gene regulatory mechanisms with a knowledge-informed cross-species foundation model
also.abstract: Deciphering universal gene regulatory mechanisms in diverse organisms holds great potential for advancing our knowledge of fundamental life processes and facilitating clinical applications. However, the traditional research paradigm primarily focuses on individual model organisms and does not integrate various cell types across species. Recent breakthroughs in single-cell sequencing and deep learning techniques present an unprecedented opportunity to address this challenge. In this study, we built an extensive dataset of over 120 million human and mouse single-cell transcriptomes. After data preprocessing, we obtained 101,768,420 single-cell transcriptomes and developed a knowledge-informed cross-species foundation model, named GeneCompass. During pre-training, GeneCompass effectively integrated four types of prior biological knowledge to enhance our understanding of gene regulatory mechanisms in a self-supervised manner. By fine-tuning for multiple downstream tasks, GeneCompass outperformed state-of-the-art models in diverse applications for a single species and unlocked new realms of cross-species biological investigations. We also employed GeneCompass to search for key factors associated with cell fate transition and showed that the predicted candidate genes could successfully induce the differentiation of human embryonic stem cells into the gonadal fate. Overall, GeneCompass demonstrates the advantages of using artificial intelligence technology to decipher universal gene regulatory mechanisms and shows tremendous potential for accelerating the discovery of critical cell fate regulators and candidate drug targets.
